title: Georgia's Governor Candidates Meet for Their Only TV Debate
summary:
This election season, 36 states across the U.S. are holding elections for governor. A governor is the leader of a state's government. One of those states is Georgia, where the two main candidates met this week for their first and only televised debate.

The candidates are Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat and former mayor of Atlanta, and Rick Jackson, a Republican businessman. Georgia is called a "purple" state, meaning it is not firmly controlled by either party. Jackson is slightly ahead in the polls right now, according to PBS NewsHour reporter Liz Landers.

The debate gave Georgia voters a chance to ask the candidates questions directly. Many topics were the same ones being discussed across the country. They included the cost of living, Flock cameras that read car license plates and are common in Atlanta, data centers, wage growth and expanding Medicaid, a government health insurance program.

Bottoms tried to connect Jackson to President Donald Trump. She said Jackson had claimed there was not a single policy he disagreed with Trump on. "My number one priority is Georgians," she said.

Jackson did not mention Trump by name. Instead, he compared himself to Georgia's current Republican governor, Brian Kemp. Trump has endorsed Jackson, though Jackson has not talked about that much lately.

Landers attended a watch party held by Republicans in Fulton County. Supporters there said they liked Jackson's business background and that he is not a longtime politician. Jackson also has a large money advantage and is running many TV ads.

Across the country, there are currently 26 Republican governors and 24 Democratic governors. Both parties see chances to win some governor races that the other party now holds.
why_it_matters: Governors make decisions about schools, roads and health programs, so these elections shape daily life in each state. Debates give voters a direct way to compare candidates.

background_read: A governor is the elected leader of a U.S. state, somewhat like a president for one state.
Governors are chosen by voters, and candidates often hold debates so voters can compare their ideas side by side.
Most U.S. candidates belong to one of two big political parties, the Democrats or the Republicans.
A purple state is one where voters are fairly evenly split between those two parties, so elections there can be close.
